ISO C has evolved over nearly forty years of the standards process, diverging from Kernighan and Ritchie C (K&RC) and becoming poorly suited to operating system development.
Operating system programming continues to be done in non-ISO dialects of C, relying on compiler-specific opt-outs, assembler escapes, and coding tricks.

The rationale for the C standard cited C's capability to function as a 'high-level assembler' and explained that many operations are defined by how the target machine's hardware does it rather than by a general abstract rule.
ISO C delegates a great deal of control to the compiler, not the programmer, environment, or target architecture, which has damaging effects on reliability and expressive range for OS programming.
The ISO approach of delegating to the compiler has led to optimizations that can break otherwise correct code, such as deleting null pointer checks or optimizing away pointer equality comparisons.
The loss of semantic clarity in ISO C has left many specific questions unclear about what programming idioms are allowed and what compiler alias analysis and optimization are permitted.
The C18 standard document includes a 10-page, incomplete list of undefined behaviors, covering everything from type constraints to syntax errors and synchronization errors.
Most C programs, especially operating system code, contain undefined behavior, making C compilers unstable and introducing landmines in code.

Operating system developers often resort to compiler-specific flags to force certain behaviors, such as 'wrapping semantics' for arithmetic overflow, and use workarounds like disabling strict aliasing analysis.
The malloc/free implementation in K&R C is not conformant ISO C code, as ISO C requires special rules around 'effective types' to permit such functions.

Strict aliasing rules in ISO C prevent accessing an object of one type via a pointer of a different type, which is incompatible with the way operating systems often need to access the same block of storage with different types for different kernel components.
Pointer equality comparison in ISO C can be affected by compiler optimizations, such as treating two pointers with the same address but different provenance as unequal.
